title: Can both pairs of arcs be drawn on one side of X Y?
description: A question from the book asks whether the second pair of arcs must be drawn below the segment. Two pairs of arcs with different radii are drawn on one side, and the same two congruent triangle pairs show that the line through the two meeting points is still the perpendicular bisector.
teaching_notes: One idea: each meeting point is equally far from X and Y, so each lies on the perpendicular bisector, wherever it is drawn. Watch for students who think the second point must lie on the opposite side.

video_script.why: The child has drawn one pair of arcs above and one below, and has not yet asked whether the second pair may sit on the same side.
video_script.substitution: The construction is done in the same way as the example in the book, with the second pair of arcs above the segment too, and then the triangles explain why it still works.
video_script.anchor: Can both pairs of arcs be constructed on the same side of X Y?
video_script.payoff_line: No, both pairs of arcs can be on the same side

final_answer.value: No. Both pairs can be on the same side if the two radii are different; each meeting point is equally far from X and Y, so both lie on the perpendicular bisector (SSS, then SAS), and the line through them, extended, is the perpendicular bisector
final_answer.spoken: no, both pairs of arcs can be on the same side, if the two radii are different, and the line through the two meeting points is the perpendicular bisector

maths_rules: Radius r from X and from Y above XY, r more than half of XY, meets at A: AX = AY = r.
A larger radius s, above XY again, meets at P: PX = PY = s. If s = r the arcs meet at A again, so the radii must differ.
Triangle APX is congruent to triangle APY by SSS (AX = AY, PX = PY, AP common), so angle XAP = angle YAP.

Line AP extended meets XY at O; angle XAO = 180 degrees minus angle XAP and angle YAO = 180 degrees minus angle YAP, so they are equal. Triangle AOX is congruent to triangle AOY by SAS, so OX = OY and angle AOX = angle AOY = 90 degrees.
A and P are each equally far from X and Y, so both lie on the perpendicular bisector, and two points fix one line.
video_script.design: One idea: both meeting points can lie on one side if the two radii are different. The construction of the book's example is repeated, and the same two congruences explain it.
